summary.text: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, set on a walled platform in the plains of Marvdasht in Fars province, Iran.
Its palace complex and citadel served as a focal point for governance and ceremony, and its earliest remains date to 515 BC.
Alexander the Great's army took it in 330 BC and fire soon destroyed its wooden parts, and its exact function remains unclear.

items.prompt: Why do scholars hesitate to call Persepolis an ordinary city?

options.label: It was larger than every other city in Iran
Its buildings were all made of mud brick
It was only ever a military camp
It seems a seasonal ceremonial site; permanent buildings are unclear

items.explain: It was not among the largest cities, appears to have been a ceremonial site occupied seasonally, and it is unclear what permanent structures stood outside the palaces.

items.prompt: Stairway reliefs show nobles and subject peoples bringing gifts to the king. What occasion did most archaeologists long think the site mainly served?

options.label: Celebrating Nowruz, the Persian New Year
Crowning each new king
Mourning a dead king
Gathering the army before campaigns

items.explain: Until recently most archaeologists held it was primarily used for celebrating Nowruz, when nobles and tributary peoples came to present gifts.

items.prompt: Why were the Greeks unfamiliar with Persepolis until Alexander took and plundered it?

options.label: It was kept secret under penalty of death
Probably because the real capitals were Susa, Babylon and Ecbatana
It had been built only a year earlier
It was a Greek colony known by another name

items.explain: The empire's true capitals were Susa, Babylon and Ecbatana, which may be why the Greeks did not know Persepolis.

items.prompt: One theory explains the fire at Persepolis as Alexander's deliberate act. What was its motive?

options.label: To stop the Persians returning
To pay his troops with the city's gold
To avenge the Persians' destruction of Athens
To hide that his army had looted the Treasury

items.explain: One theory holds that Alexander deliberately set the fire to avenge the destruction of Athens by the Persians.

items.prompt: Scholars studying trilingual royal inscriptions from the ruins made a breakthrough in reading which ancient writing?

options.label: Cuneiform
Egyptian hieroglyphs
Linear B
Old Latin

items.explain: Exploring Persepolis led to the modern rediscovery of cuneiform and, through the trilingual royal inscriptions, its initial decipherment.

items.prompt: Who ordered the Apadana, the Council Hall and the main Treasury built?

options.label: Cyrus the Great
Xerxes I
Alexander the Great
Darius I

items.explain: Darius I ordered their construction, and they were completed under his son Xerxes I.

paragraphs.heading: A ceremonial capital
paragraphs.text: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, which lasted from about 550 to 330 BC. Its ruins stand on the Marvdasht plains in the Fars province of Iran, ringed by the southern Zagros Mountains. A palace complex and a citadel stood there, planned as the hub of government and ceremony for the empire. The site shows off the Achaemenid way of building, and today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Iran's key cultural places.

paragraphs.heading: Many names
paragraphs.text: The name Persepolis is Greek and means "the city of the Persians". The ancient Persians called it Pārsa, the same word they used for the region of Persia. In 311 AD a Sasanian prince left an inscription calling it Sad-stūn, "Hundred Pillars". Medieval Persians credited the ruins to Jamshid, a king from Iranian myth, so it became Takht-e-Jamshid, the "Throne of Jamshid"; it was also called Čehel Menâr, "Forty Minarets".

paragraphs.heading: Who built it
paragraphs.text: The oldest remains on the site go back to 515 BC. André Godard, the French archaeologist who dug there in the early 1930s, thought Cyrus the Great picked the spot but Darius I built the terrace and the palaces. Inscriptions on the buildings back up the idea that Darius built them. He ordered the Apadana, the Council Hall and the main treasury, and his son Xerxes I finished them. Work on a wide stairway began around 519 BC, grey limestone was the main stone, and building on the terrace went on until the empire fell.

paragraphs.heading: A puzzle about its purpose
paragraphs.text: No one knows exactly what Persepolis was for. It was not among the biggest cities of ancient Iran; it looks more like a grand ceremonial complex used only in certain seasons, set high on a walled platform with five halls of different sizes and grand entrances. Even the king's private rooms have not been pinned down, and it is unclear what lasting buildings stood outside the palaces, so scholars usually call it a complex rather than a city. Until recently most archaeologists thought it served mainly to celebrate Nowruz, the Persian New Year, which falls at the spring equinox. Reliefs on its stairways show nobles and subject lands bringing gifts to the king.

paragraphs.heading: Captives on the road
paragraphs.text: In 330 BC Alexander the Great invaded and sent the bulk of his army toward Persepolis along the Royal Road. The writer Diodorus Siculus says that on the way they met 800 Greek craftsmen held captive by the Persians. Most were old and had been maimed, some missing a hand or a foot. They said the Persians had done this to use their skills while making escape hard. Alexander and his officers, troubled, gave them clothes and supplies. Diodorus does not name this as a reason for what came next, but it may have turned Alexander against the city.

paragraphs.heading: Battle and fire
paragraphs.text: At the Persian Gates, a pass through the Zagros Mountains, Ariobarzanes of Persis ambushed Alexander's army and inflicted heavy losses. He held them back for 31 days before Alexander got around the defenders and wiped them out. Alexander's army then took the complex, and soon after, fire destroyed all of its wooden parts. One theory says Alexander burned it on purpose as revenge for the Persian destruction of Athens. Another says a courtesan named Thaïs urged him on at a feast while he was drunk.

paragraphs.heading: Unlocking an old script
paragraphs.text: The ruins later helped people read cuneiform again. Explorers began studying Persepolis in the early 17th century, and their work brought cuneiform writing back to modern attention. Royal inscriptions on the ruins were written in three languages, and close study of them led to the first decipherment of cuneiform in the early 19th century.
